chapters.title: Welcome to Mount Olympus
chapters.narration: Way up above the clouds — higher than birds, higher than kites, higher than even the tallest mountain — there is a place called Mount Olympus. And on Mount Olympus, the gods live. Now, most people think the gods are very serious, very powerful, and very grown-up. Most people have never met Little Zeus. Because Little Zeus is eight years old. And he is about to have the WORST morning of his entire life. Every single morning, Little Zeus did the exact same thing. First, he jumped out of bed. Then he ate twelve breakfast olives — don't judge him, that's normal on Olympus. Then he put on his tiny golden crown — which always went on sideways no matter what he did. And then, finally, he checked on his thunderbolt. The thunderbolt was his most prized possession. His dad had given it to him. It lived on a special golden stand right next to his bed. It was always there. Always. Until today. The stand was empty. Little Zeus stared at it. He blinked. He rubbed his eyes. He looked behind the stand. He looked UNDER the stand. He looked inside his pillow. He looked inside his twelve breakfast olives. The thunderbolt was GONE. Not misplaced. Not hiding. Gone. And here is the thing you need to understand about a thunderbolt: it is not just a cool glowing stick. It controls all the lightning in the world. Without it, no storms. No lightning. No electricity. Which means — no toasted olives. This was a crisis.

chapters.title: The Great Search Begins
chapters.narration: Little Zeus searched every single corner of his palace. He checked the throne room. He checked the kitchen. He checked the room where they kept all the clouds. He even checked the room that nobody was supposed to go in — the one with the label that said 'ABSOLUTELY NO THUNDERBOLTS IN HERE, WE MEAN IT.' It was not there either. He was running out of places to look. And he was running out of ideas. Which meant it was time to do the one thing every hero does when they run out of ideas: go find their friends. Zeus's first stop was the workshop of Hephaestus — the god of the forge, and the person who had actually built the thunderbolt in the first place. Hephaestus was very busy. He was building something extremely large that appeared to be on fire, which was normal for his workshop. He listened very carefully to Zeus's problem. Then he said, very helpfully: 'Have you checked behind the sofa?' Zeus had not checked behind the sofa. He went back and checked behind the sofa. It was not there. He had also found three drachmas and a very old sandwich. Not helpful. Zeus's next stop was the ocean palace of his uncle Poseidon — god of the sea. Poseidon was also very busy. He was reorganizing which direction all the waves went, which apparently takes enormous concentration. Zeus explained the situation about the missing thunderbolt. Poseidon scratched his enormous beard thoughtfully. Then he said: 'I once lost my trident for three whole weeks. It was inside a whale the whole time. Have you checked inside a whale?' Zeus had not checked inside a whale. Zeus was not going to check inside a whale. This was not the help he needed.

chapters.title: Baby Hercules to the Rescue (Sort Of)
chapters.narration: There was one more friend to try: Baby Hercules. Zeus found him in the garden. Baby Hercules was the strongest child who had ever lived or would ever live. He was so strong that by accident, before breakfast, he had already picked up a very large boulder, thrown it into the sea, and accidentally given three dolphins a very exciting morning. When Zeus told him about the missing thunderbolt, Hercules's face lit up. He loved solving problems. He was absolutely terrible at solving problems. But he loved it. He cracked his enormous little knuckles. 'I'll help,' he said. Zeus immediately felt both better and worse. Hercules's idea was to search the whole garden by picking up everything in it and shaking it, to see if the thunderbolt fell out. This worked in the sense that they found seven lost sandals, a map nobody recognized, and something that turned out to be a very confused hedgehog. It did not work in the sense of finding the thunderbolt. It did work in the sense of rearranging the entire garden into a completely different shape, which the garden had opinions about. There was a lot of yelling, mostly from the flowers. This is why Baby Hercules always needs supervision. Unfortunately, he had none. Zeus and Hercules found Athena sitting calmly on the steps of the library, reading a scroll. She did not look up when they arrived. She did not look up when Hercules tripped over a step and fell down with a noise like a thousand pots falling down a staircase. She simply said, turning a page: 'I know about the thunderbolt. I've been watching the storm clouds since dawn. Sit down. Both of you. There's something you need to see.' Zeus sat down immediately. Hercules sat down so hard the steps cracked a little. Athena finally looked up. She pointed at the sky. And there — in the middle of an enormous dark storm cloud — was a golden glow.

chapters.title: Meet Stormy the Storm Cloud
chapters.narration: The cloud's name was Stormy. Athena had already looked him up in her encyclopedia of weather phenomena, which she carried everywhere, because of course she did. Stormy was one of the oldest storm clouds on Olympus. He had been making lightning and rain for two hundred years. He knew every part of the sky. He had seen every season. And lately, nobody had noticed him at all. Not the gods. Not the people below. Nobody looked up anymore. Nobody thanked him for the rain. Nobody jumped in his puddles. So Stormy had done something drastic. He had borrowed the one thing guaranteed to make everyone pay attention. Zeus had a plan. It was a very straightforward plan. He would fly up to the cloud, ask for the thunderbolt back nicely, and that would be that. He took a running start. He jumped. He flew upward with great confidence and excellent hair. He reached Stormy. He said, in his most kingly voice: 'Please give it back.' Stormy stared at him for three full seconds. Then Stormy breathed in. And blew Zeus all the way back to the ground with a gust of wind so powerful it rearranged his curls in a direction they had never been in before. So that plan didn't work. Baby Hercules had a different approach. His approach was: if the cloud won't come to you, you climb to the cloud. He found the tallest tree on Olympus. It was five hundred meters tall. He climbed to the top. He reached up. He was still very far from the cloud. He stretched. He stretched some more. His arm made a very concerning noise. He almost touched it. Almost. And then the tree, which had been extremely patient up to this point, decided it had had enough, and very slowly leaned him sideways until he fell off. He was fine. He broke a medium-sized hill. The hill was also fine. Mostly.

chapters.title: The Problem Is Bigger Than They Thought
chapters.narration: Zeus and Hercules sat on what was left of the hill and thought about this. Without the thunderbolt, the storms wouldn't come. Without storms, there'd be no rain. Without rain, the crops wouldn't grow. The rivers would start to slow. The flowers would start to droop. All of Greece would look up and wonder what had happened to the sky. This wasn't just Zeus's problem anymore. This was everybody's problem. And the more Zeus thought about it, the more he realized something: he'd been thinking about the thunderbolt like it was his thing. But really, it belonged to everyone. He just carried it. Athena sat down with them. She didn't say 'I told you so,' which was very restrained of her. Instead she asked a question: 'Why do you think Stormy took it?' Zeus said because Stormy was mean. Hercules said because clouds are bad. Athena shook her head. She pointed to her scroll. In her two hundred years of observation, she said, Stormy had never done anything like this before. Not once. That meant something had changed. Something had upset him. And things that upset people — or clouds — don't get fixed by force or by shouting. They get fixed by listening. Zeus felt something uncomfortable happen in his chest. It was called understanding someone else's feelings. It was new for him. Zeus went quiet for a moment. He remembered his first week on Olympus. He was the new king. Everyone knew who he was. But knowing who someone is isn't the same as knowing them. He remembered eating his olives alone for three days before Hercules came and sat down next to him without asking. He remembered how much that had mattered. The thunderbolt was powerful. But the thing that had actually made Olympus feel like home — that was something else. Maybe Stormy just needed someone to come and sit down next to him. Even if he was a cloud. Even if he was a grumpy one.

chapters.title: The Real Plan
chapters.narration: The new plan was completely different. No more flying up and demanding. No more trying to pull the cloud down. This time, they were going to go up together. All three of them. And they were going to ask Stormy — really ask him — what was wrong. Athena had prepared a small speech. Hercules had prepared a wave. Zeus had prepared to actually listen, which for him was genuinely the hardest thing on the list. They borrowed three small personal clouds from the cloud storage room — which still had the sign saying no thunderbolts, which in hindsight was quite ironic — and they floated up. Stormy saw them coming. He pulled himself together — which for a storm cloud means getting bigger and darker and crackle-ier. He was ready to blow them away again. He was ready to be absolutely impossible about this. But then something unexpected happened. Instead of demanding, instead of threatening, Little Zeus held up his hand and said just four words: 'We want to talk.' And then he waited. He didn't push forward. He didn't shout. He just waited. Stormy had been expecting a fight. He had not been expecting patience. He didn't know what to do with patience. His lightning dimmed. Just a little. Stormy talked for a long time. It came out a bit like a storm — big and loud and a little chaotic. He talked about two hundred years of making rain that nobody thanked. He talked about farmers who used to look up and wave at the sky, and how they'd stopped. He talked about children who used to run outside when it rained and jump in puddles, and how now they stayed inside. He talked about being replaced in everyone's mind with sunshine, as if rain wasn't just as important, as if he didn't matter. His lightning crackled the whole time, but quieter. Not angry lightning. Sad lightning. There is a difference.

chapters.title: Zeus Actually Listens
chapters.narration: Zeus had never listened to a cloud before. He wasn't totally sure he knew how. But he listened. He heard the part about the farmers stopping waving. He heard the part about the puddles. He heard the part about being invisible even though you're enormous and right there in the sky. And he realized something: he had a thunderbolt that made everyone pay attention to him wherever he went. He had never had to wonder if anyone noticed him. Stormy had never had that. Not once. For two hundred years. Zeus put his crown on the railing of his little cloud. He said, very quietly: 'I'm sorry. That sounds really lonely.' Zeus had an idea. Not a kingly idea. A friend idea. He asked Stormy: what if, every Tuesday, it rained on Olympus? Not a little drizzle. Proper rain. The kind with puddles. The kind that farmers look up and cheer about. The kind that children run outside for. He would make sure everyone on Olympus knew that Tuesday rain came from Stormy. That Stormy was important. Not invisible. Important. Stormy looked at him for a long time. His lightning completely stopped. And then Stormy said, in a voice like distant thunder: 'Can the puddles be really big ones?' Zeus said absolutely yes. Hercules said he would personally jump in every single one. Stormy said okay. The thunderbolt floated down into Zeus's hands. Stormy kept his promise immediately. Right there. Right then. He opened up and let it pour. And it was the absolute best rain that had ever fallen on Mount Olympus in two hundred years. The kind of rain that smells like the world getting clean. The kind of rain that turns a whole mountain into one giant puddle opportunity. Baby Hercules jumped into the first puddle so hard the splash went all the way to Athens, where three very confused citizens looked up and got completely soaked and had absolutely no idea why. Athena's owl got wet and became extremely thin and extremely grumpy, which was funny to everyone except the owl.

chapters.title: Stormy Becomes Part of the Team
chapters.narration: From that day on, Stormy was an official part of the Olympus crew. He got his own spot in the sky, right above the garden, where everyone could see him. Every Tuesday it rained. Every Tuesday, the farmers waved up at the sky. Every Tuesday, children ran outside for puddles. Every Tuesday, Stormy glowed just a little less grey and just a little more silver-blue — the color clouds turn when they're actually happy, if you know what to look for. And Hercules, true to his word, jumped in every single puddle. Every one. Even the tiny ones. Especially the tiny ones. And here is what Little Zeus learned that day. He had the most powerful weapon in the entire world. And the thing that actually solved the problem was putting it down and listening. Being the king of the gods doesn't mean you never need to understand how someone else feels. It means you do it first. The strongest thing you can do is sometimes the quietest one. Not bad for a morning that started with twelve olives and a missing thunderbolt. Not bad at all. That's it for today's adventure on Little Olympus! Next time — Baby Hercules meets a GIANT SNAKE. Which sounds dangerous. And it is. But Baby Hercules has the opposite problem of what you'd expect, because Baby Hercules always does. Subscribe so you don't miss it! And if you have a friend who might need someone to sit with them at lunch — maybe do that today. Zeus would. He learned. See you next time on Little Olympus!
